:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
The equation $x^2-2x+y^2+4y=5$ represents a circle. The normal line at the point $\left(0, -5 \right)$ on the circle intersects the $x$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$

![](images/b6/b6c52a76654a4a545d356890d4deb04c74301e4091422a51e84551aeb3ec1152.png)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(0,-5).$ Remember that the slope of the normal line, $m',$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
m' = -\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y = y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}
	\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (x^2-2x+ y^2+4y)
	&=\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (5)\\[5pt]	
	
	\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (x^2)-\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (2x)+\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (y^2)+\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (4y)&=\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (5)\\[5pt]	
	
	2x-2+2y\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}+4\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}&=0\\[5pt]	
	
	
	(2y+4)\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}&=2-2x\\[5pt]	
	
	\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
	&=\dfrac{2-2x}{2y+4}
	
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $\left(0,\,-5 \right)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}
	m
	&=\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}\right)_{\left(0,\,-5 \right)}\\[5pt]
	&=\left(\dfrac{2-2x}{2y+4}\right)_{\left(0,\,-5 \right)}\\[5pt]
	&=\dfrac{2-2\cdot 0}{2\cdot (-5)+4}\\[5pt]
	&=\dfrac{2}{-6}\\[5pt]
	&=-\dfrac{1}{3} \, .
	
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is $m'=-\dfrac{1}{m}=3.$ We can write the equation of the normal at the point $\left(0,\,-5 \right)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
	y-y_1 &=m'\left(x-x_1 \right)\\[5pt]
	y+5 &=3\left(x-0 \right)\\[5pt]
	y&=3x-5
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $x$-axis. At the point $P$ the $y$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $y=0$ and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
	y&=3x-5\\[5pt]
	0&=3x-5\\[5pt]
	x&=\dfrac{5}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $\left(\dfrac{5}{3},\,0 \right).$

The equation $x^{2} + 4y^{2} = 6$ represents an ellipse. The normal line at the point $(\sqrt{2}, 1)$ on the ellipse intersects the $x$-axis at the point $P$. What are the coordinates of $P$?
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution: Implicit differentiation gives the tangent slope $-x/(4y)=-1/(2\sqrt2)$ at $(\sqrt2,1)$. The normal slope is its negative reciprocal, $2\sqrt2$. Thus the normal is $y-1=2\sqrt2(x-\sqrt2)$. Setting $y=0$ yields $$x=\sqrt2-\frac1{2\sqrt2}=\frac3{2\sqrt2}.$$ Therefore $P=(\tfrac3{2\sqrt2},0)$.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: The equation of a curve is $xy+{x}^{2}=1.$ The normal line at the point $(1,\,0)$ intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(1,\,0).$   Remember that the slope of the normal line, ${m}^{′},$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy+{x}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) & =0 \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y+2x & =0 \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-(2x+y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2x+y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,\,0)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(1,\,0)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{2x+y}{x}\right)}_{(1,\,0)} \\  & =-\frac{2\cdot 1+0}{1} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is $$
\displaystyle {m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{-2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$ We can write the equation of the normal at the point $(1,\,0)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & ={m}^{′}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-0) & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}(0-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,-\frac{1}{2}).$

The equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$  represents a circle. The tangent line at the point $(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2})$ on the circle intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the tangent line at the point $(\sqrt{2},\,\sqrt{2}).$ 

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2x}{2y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(\sqrt{2},\,\sqrt{2})$  is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(\sqrt{2},\,\sqrt{2})} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{x}{y}\right)}_{(\sqrt{2},\,\sqrt{2})} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can write the equation of the tangent at the point $(\sqrt{2},\,\sqrt{2})$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-\sqrt{2}) & =-1(x-\sqrt{2}) \\ y & =-(x-\sqrt{2})+\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this tangent line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-(x-\sqrt{2})+\sqrt{2} \\ y & =-(0-\sqrt{2})+\sqrt{2} \\ y & =\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{2} \\ y & =2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,2\sqrt{2}).$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}8y & ={x}^{2}+4x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+4x) \\ 8\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x+4 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2x+4}{8} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x+2}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: The equation of a curve is $3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}=9.$ The normal line at the point $(3,\,3)$ intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(3,\,3).$  Remember that the slope of the normal line, ${m}^{'},$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
{m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(9) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 6x-4y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ -4y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-6x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{-6x}{-4y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3x}{2y}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(3,\,3)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(3,\,3)} \\  & ={\left(\frac{3x}{2y}\right)}_{(3,\,3)} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 3}{2\cdot 3} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is $$
\displaystyle {m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{3/2}=-\frac{2}{3}.
$$ We can write the equation of the normal at the point $(3,\,3)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & ={m}^{'}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-3) & =-\frac{2}{3}(x-3) \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}(x-3)+3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{2}{3}(x-3)+3 \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}(0-3)+3 \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}(-3)+3 \\ y & =2+3 \\ y & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,5).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: The equation of a curve is $2{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}=8.$ The tangent line at the point $(1,\,1)$ on the curve intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the tangent line at the point $(1,\,1).$  

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 4x+12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-4x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{4x}{12y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{3y}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,1)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(1,\,1)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{x}{3y}\right)}_{(1,\,1)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3\cdot 1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can write the equation of the tangent at the point $(1,1)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-1) & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-1)+1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this tangent line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-1)+1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}(0-1)+1 \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}+1 \\ y & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,\frac{4}{3}).$

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x-6y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ -6y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{-2x}{-6y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x}{3y}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(-3,\,1)$ is 

 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(-3,\,1)} \\  & ={\left(\frac{x}{3y}\right)}_{(-3,\,1)} \\  & =\frac{-3}{3\cdot 1} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(-4,\,0).$

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $xy$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+xy & =6{y}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+xy) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{y}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{y}^{2}) \\ 2x+(y+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) & =12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\ 2x+y+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x-y \\ (x-12y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x-y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{-2x-y}{x-12y}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,1)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(2,\,1)} \\  & ={\left(\frac{-2x-y}{x-12y}\right)|}_{(2,\,1)} \\  & =\frac{-2(2)-1}{2-12(1)} \\  & =\frac{(-5)}{(-10)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}=-2.
$$

We can write the equation of the normal at the point $(2,1)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & ={m}^{′}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =-2(x-2) \\ y-1 & =-2x+4 \\ y & =-2x+5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-2x+5 \\ y & =-2(0)+5 \\ y & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,5).$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:

Note that to differentiate the $xy$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+4) \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4x \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4x \\ (x+2y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4x-y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4x-y}{x+2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at the point $\left(1,\,2 \right)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
m
&=\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}\right)_{\left(1,\,2 \right)}\\[5pt]
&=\left(\dfrac{4x-y}{x+2y}\right)_{\left(1,\,2 \right)}\\[5pt]

\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}

	&=\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (5)\\[5pt]	
	
	\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (x^2)-\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (2x)+\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (y^2)+\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (4y)&=\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (5)\\[5pt]	
	
	2x-2+2y\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}+4\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}&=0\\[5pt]	
	
	
	(2y+4)\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}&=2-2x\\[5pt]	
	
	\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
	&=\dfrac{2-2x}{2y+4}
	
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $\left(0,\,-5 \right)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}
	m
	&=\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}\right)_{\left(0,\,-5 \right)}\\[5pt]
	&=\left(\dfrac{2-2x}{2y+4}\right)_{\left(0,\,-5 \right)}\\[5pt]
	&=\dfrac{2-2\cdot 0}{2\cdot (-5)+4}\\[5pt]
	&=\dfrac{2}{-6}\\[5pt]
	&=-\dfrac{1}{3} \, .
	
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is $m'=-\dfrac{1}{m}=3.$ We can write the equation of the normal at the point $\left(0,\,-5 \right)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
	y-y_1 &=m'\left(x-x_1 \right)\\[5pt]
	y+5 &=3\left(x-0 \right)\\[5pt]
	y&=3x-5
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $x$-axis. At the point $P$ the $y$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $y=0$ and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
	y&=3x-5\\[5pt]
	0&=3x-5\\[5pt]
	x&=\dfrac{5}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $\left(\dfrac{5}{3},\,0 \right).$

$$

$$

When a function is given in implicit form, we can differentiate it using the method of **implicit differentiation**, which consists of the following two steps:

**Step 1**: Differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x.$

We need to remember that $y$ *is a function of* $x,$ i.e., $y = y(x),$ So, we apply the chain rule:
$$
\begin{array}{cc}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} x} ( 2 {x}^{3} + {y}^{2} ) &  = \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} x} ( 3 ) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} x} ( 2 {x}^{3} ) + \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} x} ( {y}^{2} ) &  = 0 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} x} ( 2 {x}^{3} ) + \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} y} ( {y}^{2} ) ( \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x} ) &  = 0 \\ 6 {x}^{2} + 2 y \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x} &  = 0\end{array}
$$

**Step 2**: Solve the equation for $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$
$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle 6 {x}^{2} + 2 y {\displaystyle \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x}} & \displaystyle  = 0 \\ \displaystyle 2 y {\displaystyle \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x}} & \displaystyle  = - 6 {x}^{2} \\ \displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x}} & \displaystyle  = - {\displaystyle \frac{3 {x}^{2}}{y}}\end{array}
$$

So, the derivative of $y$ is $$
\displaystyle \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}=- \dfrac{3x^2}{y}.
$$

	\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (x^2)-\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (2x)+\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (y^2)+\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (4y)&=\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (5)\\[5pt]	
	
	2x-2+2y\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}+4\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}&=0\\[5pt]	
	
	
	(2y+4)\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}&=2-2x\\[5pt]	
	
	\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
	&=\dfrac{2-2x}{2y+4}
	
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $\left(0,\,-5 \right)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}
	m
	&=\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}\right)_{\left(0,\,-5 \right)}\\[5pt]
	&=\left(\dfrac{2-2x}{2y+4}\right)_{\left(0,\,-5 \right)}\\[5pt]
	&=\dfrac{2-2\cdot 0}{2\cdot (-5)+4}\\[5pt]
	&=\dfrac{2}{-6}\\[5pt]
	&=-\dfrac{1}{3} \, .
	
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is $m'=-\dfrac{1}{m}=3.$ We can write the equation of the normal at the point $\left(0,\,-5 \right)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
	y-y_1 &=m'\left(x-x_1 \right)\\[5pt]
	y+5 &=3\left(x-0 \right)\\[5pt]
	y&=3x-5
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $x$-axis. At the point $P$ the $y$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $y=0$ and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
	y&=3x-5\\[5pt]
	0&=3x-5\\[5pt]
	x&=\dfrac{5}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $\left(\dfrac{5}{3},\,0 \right).$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Determining an Intercept of a Tangent or Normal Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=x^3 - x^2$ at the point $(1,0)$ is given by $y=px+q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the values of $p$ and $q.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=x^3 - x^2.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-{x}^{2})=3{x}^{2}-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1, 0){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=3-2=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line $m'$ is

$$
m'=-\dfrac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-0 & =-(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-1$ and $q=1.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y = 2x^3 -x^2$ at the point $(1,1).$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x) = 2x^3-x^2.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
f'(x)  =6x^2 -2x
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
m=f'(1) = 6(1)^2 - 2(1) = 4
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line $m'$ is

$$
m' = -\dfrac{1}{m} = -\dfrac 1 4.
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating the Slope of a Normal Line to a Curve at a Point

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x) = 2\sqrt{x} -4x$ at the point $(1,-2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}-4x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{1/2}-4x) \\  & ={x}^{-1/2}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

     

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1) = (1)^{-1/2} - 4 = -3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m' = -\dfrac{1}{m} = \dfrac 1 3.
$$

The equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-2) & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y+2 & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{1}{3}-2 \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{3}x & =\frac{7}{3} \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(7,0).$
